title: Exploring Plain Vision Transformer Backbones for Object Detection

problem.summary: Object detection has been built around hierarchical, multi-scale backbones because ConvNets are hierarchical, which entrenched FPN-style neck/head designs; the plain (non-hierarchical, single-scale) ViT is hard to fine-tune for detection because it lacks multi-scale maps, global self-attention over high-resolution images is prohibitive, and redesigning backbones into hierarchies couples pre-training to detection.
statements: For a long while backbones have been multi-scale, hierarchical architectures due to the de facto ConvNet design, which heavily influenced neck/head designs such as FPN.

It is unclear how to address multi-scale objects in a downstream task with a plain backbone from upstream pre-training, and whether a plain ViT is too inefficient for high-resolution detection images.
Global self-attention throughout the backbone on high-resolution detection inputs is prohibitive in memory and slow.
Redesigning Transformer backbones into hierarchies (e.g., Swin) couples the pre-training architecture to detection fine-tuning, breaking the decoupling enjoyed by ConvNet research.

evidence.quote: For a long while, these backbones have been multi-scale, hierarchical architectures due to the de facto design of convolutional networks (ConvNet) [32], which has heavily influenced the neck/head design for detecting objects at multiple scales (e.g., FPN).
How can we address multi-scale objects in a downstream task with a plain backbone from upstream pre-training?
Object detectors benefit from high-resolution input images, but computing global self-attention throughout the backbone is prohibitive in memory and is slow.

background.summary: Covers the pretrain-then-finetune detector paradigm (R-CNN, Fast/Faster R-CNN), FPN as the standard pyramid on hierarchical backbones, single-scale revisits (Trident Networks, YOLOF), hierarchical Transformers (Swin, MViT, PVT, PiT), and the plain-backbone competitor UViT; the study targets the original plain ViT with Mask R-CNN/Cascade/RetinaNet heads.

relatedWork.name: FPN
relatedWork.relation: standard in-network pyramid that assumes a hierarchical backbone
relatedWork.quote: The FPN design is widely used in object detection methods.

relatedWork.name: Swin / MViT / PVT / PiT
relatedWork.relation: hierarchical Transformers that re-introduce multi-scale structure to inherit ConvNet detector designs
relatedWork.quote: These methods inherit some designs from ConvNets, including the hierarchical structure and the translation-equivariant priors (e.g., convolutions, pooling, sliding windows).

relatedWork.name: UViT
relatedWork.relation: concurrent plain-backbone detector that modifies the architecture during pre-training
relatedWork.quote: Unlike UViT that modifies the architecture during pre-training, our study focuses on the original ViT architecture without a priori specification for detection.

relatedWork.name: MAE
relatedWork.relation: self-supervised pre-training that supplies the plain ViT backbones used for detection
relatedWork.quote: In this study, our plain-backbone detector has benefited from the readily available pretrained models from MAE [24].

evidence.quote: Our method decouples the backbone design from the detection task, which is a key motivation of pursuing plain backbones.
our detector builds a simple feature pyramid from only the last feature map of a plain ViT backbone

solution.summary: ViTDet adapts a plain ViT to detection only at fine-tuning time: a simple feature pyramid built by parallel strided convolutions/deconvolutions from the single 1/16-scale last feature map (no FPN top-down/lateral connections), non-overlapping window attention for high-resolution maps with a few (default 4) evenly placed cross-window propagation blocks (global attention or zero-initialized conv residual blocks), and standard Mask R-CNN/Cascade heads on MAE-pre-trained ViT-B/L/H backbones.
solution.approach: Keep the original ViT architecture untouched by pre-training, then add only minimal fine-tuning-time modules: a simple single-scale-origin pyramid, window attention with sparse cross-window propagation, and conventional detection heads.
components: simple feature pyramid from the last 1/16 feature map, producing scales {1/32, 1/16, 1/8, 1/4} via parallel stride-{2, 1, 1/2, 1/4} convolutions/deconvolutions (fractional stride = deconvolution)
non-overlapping window self-attention during fine-tuning, without Swin-style shifting
4 cross-window propagation blocks placed evenly: global self-attention in the last block of each subset, or added conv residual blocks initialized to identity
MAE pre-training on ImageNet-1K without labels as the backbone initialization
Mask R-CNN / Cascade Mask R-CNN / RetinaNet heads with large-scale jittering at 1024x1024 input
relative position biases added only during fine-tuning for comparisons

evidence.quote: This abandons the FPN design [37] and waives the requirement of a hierarchical backbone.
To efficiently extract features from high-resolution images, our detector uses simple non-overlapping window attention (without “shifting”, unlike [42]).
A small number of cross-window blocks (e.g., 4), which could be global attention [54] or convolutions, are used to propagate information.
These adaptations are made only during fine-tuning and do not alter pre-training.
Our ablation reveals that the set of pyramidal feature maps, rather than the top-down/lateral connections, is the key to effective multi-scale detection.

experiments.summary: Ablations on COCO train2017/val2017 (pyramid design, propagation strategy/location/count, pre-training recipe) with Mask R-CNN; controlled backbone comparisons against Swin and MViTv2 in the same implementation for Mask R-CNN and Cascade Mask R-CNN; system-level comparisons on COCO (with soft-nms and 1280 input) and on LVIS v1 val, plus a RetinaNet-head transfer study in the appendix.

benchmarks.split: Cascade, ViTDet ViT-H, multi-scale test, 1K MAE (Table 6)

evidence.quote: We train on the train2017 split and evaluate on the val2017 split.
In contrast, MAE [24] pre-training on IN-1K (without labels) shows massive gains, increasing APbox by 3.1 for ViT-B and 4.6 for ViT-L.
Our result with ViT-H is 2.6 better than that with MViTv2-H.
For the first time, we show that a plain-backbone detector can achieve highly accurate results on COCO and can compete with the leading systems.
Ours is 5.0 points higher than the 2021 competition winner’s “strong baseline” [18] (48.1 vs. 43.1 APmask )

limitations.summary: Study scope is deliberately narrow: long-tailed LVIS issues, MAE recipes for hierarchical backbones, and detection-head inductive biases are out of scope; full global attention needs memory optimization and does not scale; system-level comparisons cannot be perfectly controlled, and the plain backbone still needs a few propagation blocks plus a pyramid to work well.
items: Global self-attention in all 24 ViT-L blocks requires special memory optimization and is impractical for scaling to larger models such as ViT-H.
Exploiting the long-tailed class distribution of LVIS (e.g., CLIP text embeddings, rare-class techniques) is beyond the scope of the study.
Exploring detectors with even fewer inductive biases (beyond standard Mask R-CNN heads) is left as open future work.

evidence.quote: This requirement makes scaling to larger models (like ViT-H) impractical.
A special issue in LVIS is on the long-tailed distribution, which is beyond the scope of our study.
Exploring even fewer inductive biases in the detection heads is an open and interesting direction for future work.

futureDirections.direction: Pursue detection heads with fewer inductive biases, building on the plain-backbone approach.
futureDirections.quote: Exploring even fewer inductive biases in the detection heads is an open and interesting direction for future work.

futureDirections.direction: Improve hierarchical backbones with MAE pre-training as a future research topic.
futureDirections.quote: While it is an interesting future topic on improving hierarchical backbones with MAE pre-training, our plain-backbone detector enables us to use the readily available ViT backbones from MAE to achieve strong results.

futureDirections.direction: Spread the decoupling of pre-training from fine-tuning as a general methodology, drawing NLP parallels (GPT, BERT).
futureDirections.quote: We hope decoupling pre-training from fine-tuning is a methodology that will generally benefit the community.

applications.domain: general-purpose ViT backbone reuse for detection systems
applications.detail: Decoupling pre-training from fine-tuning lets detection use any available or improved plain ViT (new block designs, self-supervised models, scaling) without re-architecting the backbone for multi-scale hierarchies.
applications.quote: This makes our detector compatible with ViT developments along various directions that are not necessarily limited by the hierarchical constraint, e.g., block designs [52,53], self-supervised learning [2,24], and scaling [57].

deploymentClaims: Convolutional propagation increases training memory and test time by at most 5%, at a 4% parameter cost.
Global propagation with 4 blocks does not increase model size; window attention plus a few propagation blocks is a practical, high-performing tradeoff.
Testing time for the ViT-L based detector is benchmarked per image on an A100 GPU (88 ms baseline in Table 3).
Plain ViT blocks are more hardware-friendly, giving better wall-clock performance than MViTv2-H at ViT-H scale.
Code for ViTDet is available in detectron2.

evidence.quote: Convolutional propagation is the most practical, increasing memory and time by merely ≤5%, at a small cost of 4% more parameters.
the plain ViT has a better wall-clock performance (Figure 3 right, see ViT-H vs. MViTv2-H), as the simpler blocks are more hardware-friendly.
The testing time (per image) is benchmarked on an A100 GPU.
